explanations.explanation: That's what Mary sees, and it's the first thing that tells her something is off. She gets there while it's still dark, and the stone is no longer at the entrance (John 20:1). Imagine walking up to your own front door in the dark and the door is just GONE. Friend, I think she stopped dead in her tracks.

explanations.answer: The stone is still in place
explanations.explanation: That would be the normal thing to find, but it's not what Mary finds. John 20:1 says she "…saw that the stone had been removed from the entrance." The stone isn't sitting there blocking anything. The text says it was removed, so the entrance is open when she arrives.

Cracked would be a dramatic detail, but the text never says it. John 20:1 says she saw that the stone had been "…removed from the entrance." Removed, not cracked, not smashed. The entrance is open when she arrives.

Not quite, friend. Mary says the opposite. She tells them, "They have taken the Lord out of the tomb, and we do not know where they have put Him!" (John 20:2). So she has no idea where the body is, and she comes running to Peter and the other disciple with that news.

Right, because Mary doesn't know at all. She says, "They have taken the Lord out of the tomb, and we do not know where they have put Him!" (John 20:2). She's missing the answer, and she runs to tell Peter and the other disciple anyway. Ever sprint to tell somebody a problem you can't solve yet? That's Mary.

Yes, he wins it. John 20:4 says the two were running together, but the other disciple outran Peter and reached the tomb first. No trophy is mentioned, but I'd print one. I'd just hop slowly toward it.

Peter's in the race, but he doesn't win it. The text says the other disciple "…outran Peter and reached the tomb first." (John 20:4). Peter arrives just after him (John 20:6). Second place, but he's still right there.
They start out running together, so I get why you'd pick it. But it doesn't end in a tie. John 20:4 says the other disciple outran Peter and reached the tomb first. Peter shows up just after him.
That's it. He bends down and looks in at the linen cloths lying there, but he does not go in (John 20:5). He stops at the door and peeks. Friend, we've ALL done the careful peek before the big step.

Careful, this one is true. John 20:5 says he bent down and looked in at the linen cloths, "…but he did not go in." He stays at the entrance for now. Peter is the one who walks right in next (John 20:6).

Yes, the head. John 20:7 says the cloth that had been around Jesus' head was rolled up, lying separate from the linen cloths. It's a small detail, but the writer thought it was worth including. I think Peter noticed that cloth sitting off by itself.

Feet show up in this chapter, but not here. The cloth in John 20:7 is the one that had been around Jesus' head. The feet come up later, when Mary sees the two angels, one at the head and the other at the feet (John 20:12).

Hands aren't mentioned with this cloth. John 20:7 says it's the cloth that had been around Jesus' head, rolled up and lying separate from the linen cloths. I use my mustache as hands, so I'm a little sensitive about this one.
That's right. John 20:8 says he "…saw and believed." He sees the tomb for himself, and belief follows. Notice the verse stops there and doesn't spell out more.
Doubt would be a fair guess, but the text says something else. John 20:8 says he "…saw and believed." Nothing in the verse says he doubted.
Weeping does show up in this passage, but it's Mary's. She's the one standing outside the tomb weeping (John 20:11). For the other disciple, the text says he "…saw and believed." (John 20:8).

Not yet, friend. John 20:9 says, "For they still did not understand from the Scripture that Jesus had to rise from the dead." So at this point they haven't put it together. Seeing the empty tomb and understanding the Scripture are two different things.

Correct. John 20:9 says, "For they still did not understand from the Scripture that Jesus had to rise from the dead." They're standing in an empty tomb and the full picture hasn't clicked. I've read the instructions on a cookie box three times and still missed the point, so no judgment from me.

Yes, two angels in white. John 20:12 says she saw them sitting where the body of Jesus had lain, one at the head and the other at the feet. She came looking for a body and found two angels. Bet that was NOT on her list.

Moses and Elijah do appear in another Bible scene, on the mountain with Jesus (Matthew 17:3). But that's a different moment from this one. Here Mary sees two angels in white (John 20:12). They're sitting where the body of Jesus had lain.
Those two did take care of Jesus' body earlier. Joseph of Arimathea and Nicodemus wrapped it in linen cloths with spices (John 19:38-40). But in the tomb, Mary sees two angels in white (John 20:12).

Yes, sitting. John 20:12 says the two angels in white were sitting where the body of Jesus had lain, one at the head and the other at the feet. Mary had bent down to look into the tomb when she saw them. Sitting in that spot is quiet, and nothing in the verse says they were doing anything else.
Standing is a fair guess, since angels in stories often stand. But John 20:12 says they were "…sitting where the body of Jesus had lain…" The text gives us sitting.
Kneeling isn't what the text says. The angels in John 20:12 are sitting where the body of Jesus had lain, one at the head and the other at the feet. Nobody kneels in this verse.

explanations.answer: Someone has taken her Lord away
explanations.explanation: That's her answer. She says, "Because they have taken my Lord away, and I do not know where they have put Him" (John 20:13). She doesn't know where He is, and that's what has her weeping. I think she has one thing on her mind.

explanations.answer: She came too late for the burial
explanations.explanation: The text never says that. Mary tells the angels, "Because they have taken my Lord away, and I do not know where they have put Him" (John 20:13). Her worry is about where He is now.

explanations.answer: The stone was too heavy to move
explanations.explanation: The stone is mentioned, but not like this. Mary has already seen it removed (John 20:1). When the angels ask why she's weeping, she says, "Because they have taken my Lord away…" (John 20:13).

Not this time, friend. John 20:14 says she turned around and saw Jesus standing there, "But she did not recognize that it was Jesus." So the recognition doesn't come right away. The text doesn't say why, so I won't guess either.
Right. She sees Him standing there, but John 20:14 says she "…did not recognize that it was Jesus." She looks right at Him and doesn't know Him yet. The text doesn't say why, so I'll leave that open.

Yes, the gardener. John 20:15 says she was "Thinking He was the gardener…" So she asks Him where the body has been put. She doesn't recognize Him yet (John 20:14), and a man standing there is who she takes Him to be.
A guard is a reasonable guess for a tomb, but the text doesn't say that. John 20:15 says she was "Thinking He was the gardener…" That's who she's speaking to, as far as she knows.
Priest isn't what the text says. John 20:15 says Mary was "Thinking He was the gardener…" She talks to Him as a stranger who might know where the body is.
Her name, and that's all it takes. Jesus says, "Mary" (John 20:16). One word, and she turns. I've had my name called across a bakery before, but never like THAT.

Peace is a good guess, but it isn't the word here. With Mary, Jesus says one word, and it's her name: "Mary" (John 20:16). That's the moment she turns and says, "Rabboni!" It's a name, not a greeting.
Close, because He did call her that. In John 20:15, Jesus asks, "Woman, why are you weeping?" But the one word in John 20:16 is her name: "Mary." That's the moment she turns.
That's right. Jesus says, "But go and tell My brothers…" (John 20:17). He gives her a message to carry. She's sent, and she goes.
Staying put isn't what Jesus tells her. He says, "But go and tell My brothers…" (John 20:17). He sends her out to the others.

explanations.answer: Keep it a secret for now
explanations.explanation: No secret here, friend. Jesus says, "But go and tell My brothers…" (John 20:17). And right after, Mary "…went and announced to the disciples…" (John 20:18). Not a keep-it-quiet situation.

That's right. Jesus tells her to go and tell His brothers, "I am ascending to My Father and your Father, to My God and your God." (John 20:17). He's giving her a message to carry to them. She's the one trusted to deliver it.
This one is actually true. In John 20:17, Jesus says to tell His brothers, "I am ascending to My Father and your Father, to My God and your God." That's the message Mary is given.
Yes. Mary announces to the disciples, "I have seen the Lord!" (John 20:18). And she tells them what He had said to her. She started the morning weeping, and now she's got news.
The angels are in the story, but not like that. Mary's announcement in John 20:18 is, "I have seen the Lord!" She isn't talking about a body anymore.

That's what she was looking for earlier, when she asked the one she thought was the gardener where they had put Him (John 20:15). But her announcement in John 20:18 is, "I have seen the Lord!" She saw Him, and that's what she tells the disciples.
